fun_facts: A king mackerel can hit bursts near 70 km/h (43 mph) chasing prey, among the fastest sprint speeds measured in any bony fish -- it doesn't ambush from cover, it just runs baitfish down in open water.

It's one of only a handful of fish the FDA specifically tells pregnant women and young children to avoid entirely, in the same category as shark and swordfish: a long, slow-growing life lets mercury build up in its tissue for years before it's ever caught.

Tagging studies from the 1970s and 80s helped prove Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico king mackerel are two separate migratory stocks: the Atlantic group that passes South Carolina summers here and winters off Florida, mixing there with, but never blending into, an entirely different Gulf population.

measures.label: Fork length
measures.help: Tip of the snout to the fork of the tail, measured in a straight line.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: King mackerel cannot be sexed externally in the field; unknown is the normal answer.

not_taggable.reason: a fish in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward

must_release.reason: under South Carolina's 24-inch fork-length minimum for king mackerel in South Atlantic state and federal waters
